title: Spinoza
summary: Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher who saw the world as one single Nature (which he also called God), where everything follows necessary laws. His Ethics is a path to freedom and quiet joy through understanding yourself and the causes of your feelings.
onEmotions: Spinoza called feelings “affects” and studied them the way a geometer studies lines — without judgment. Every being strives to preserve and strengthen its existence; he called this striving by the Latin word conatus. Joy is a passage to a greater power of living and acting, sadness to a lesser one; all the other feelings are built from these two and from desire. When we don’t understand where a feeling came from, we “undergo” it, as a passion; when we grasp its causes clearly (an “adequate idea”), we become more active and more free.

anxiety.text: Spinoza promised to consider human passions “as if it were a question of lines, planes and bodies” — and he would draw anxiety as a figure with two poles, hope and fear. Right now your imagination sketches a future whose outcome is unclear, and the mind is thrown between them. Spinoza called this state “vacillation of mind” — being pulled at once by opposite affects, such as hope and fear. For Spinoza, an affect holds us most tightly when its causes are vague to us: we experience it as something that has simply crashed down on us. But once you begin to understand what it is made of, you become less of a victim and more of a participant. It means looking at your anxiety with a researcher’s curiosity: it has causes, and simply bringing them into the light already gives you a little room and air.
anxiety.practice: Picture your anxiety as a drawing in the spirit of the Ethics and name out loud three or four of its lines — the thoughts and circumstances it is made of right now. Just name them, without trying to solve anything.

quote.text: An affect which is a passion ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea of it.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

fear.text: “A free man thinks of nothing less than of death, and his wisdom is a meditation not on death but on life” — one of Spinoza’s best-known propositions. Fear is natural: every living being strives to preserve itself, and your fear is one of the ways that striving shows up. Spinoza defined fear as an inconstant sadness arising from the image of a future or past thing whose outcome we doubt. The key word is “doubt”: fear lives in the uncertainty of the imagination. Spinoza believed that a life led by fear makes us weaker, while a life led by understanding makes us stronger and calmer. This isn’t a call to forbid yourself to be afraid. Rather, it’s an invitation to gently shift your gaze from what you fear to what you love and want to keep safe; that is your conatus, your power to live.
fear.practice: What exactly do you want to protect when you’re afraid? Name it — and notice that behind your fear stands your love for something.

sadness.text: Spinoza studied sorrow and the other affects the way one studies the weather or geometric figures — without reproach and without pity, wanting only to understand. The last thing he would want is for you to be ashamed of your sadness. For him, sadness is a passage to a lesser power of acting — as if your life energy had been turned down for a while. His approach is comforting: sadness doesn’t prove that something is wrong with you; it always has causes, outer and inner. And the more clearly we see those causes, the less sadness rules over us as a blind force. Spinoza also believed that joy, even a small one, restores strength. You don’t have to fight your sadness; you can understand it — and at the same time allow yourself tiny sources of joy beside it.
sadness.practice: Notice when exactly today your sadness grew stronger, and when it eased a little. What was around you in those moments?

grief.text: When his friend Pieter Balling lost his little son, Spinoza wrote him a gentle letter — about how love binds us to those we love, even in the imagination. The weight of your grief speaks of the strength of your love. One of Spinoza’s observations has helped many people. He noticed that sadness over a lost good softens when a person begins to understand that this good could not have been kept in any way — that the loss is woven into the whole order of nature. This doesn’t cancel the pain, but it lifts from it the tormenting “what if.” Spinoza also taught us to look at things “under the aspect of eternity”: what was, truly was, and nothing can ever undo it. Your love for the one who is gone remains part of you and goes on shaping who you are becoming.
grief.practice: If a “what if…” is tormenting you, try putting that thought on paper and, next to it, everything you didn’t know back then or that wasn’t up to you.

loneliness.text: Spinoza lived modestly, almost as a hermit, in a rented room, but in the evenings he would come downstairs to smoke a pipe and talk with his landlord’s family. Loneliness hurts because people truly need one another — and he saw this as a fact of nature. He wrote that nothing is more useful to a human being than another human being who lives by reason: together, people are stronger, and their abilities add up. He also described the “imitation of the affects”: we involuntarily share the feelings of those we see as like ourselves — we rejoice in their joy and grieve in their sadness. At the same time, Spinoza invites you to remember that you are part of one Nature, tied to the world by countless threads even when no one is nearby. Connection starts small: with one shared feeling.
loneliness.practice: Remember someone whose joy once spread to you without your even trying. Could you send them, or someone else, one small message today?

quote.text: To man, then, there is nothing more useful than man.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part IV, Scholium to Proposition 18

anger.text: Once, outside a synagogue, a fanatic attacked Spinoza with a knife; Spinoza survived and, it is said, long kept the cloak with the slash in it — as a reminder. Your anger is a strong affect, and most often it arises when you have been harmed or treated unjustly. Spinoza defined anger as the desire to do harm to someone we hate, and he honestly laid out its mechanics: hatred feeds on hatred returned, and grows. But he also noticed that it can be overcome — by love and by what he called “nobility”: a striving, grounded in reason, to help others and join them to ourselves in friendship. It’s an invitation to understand its causes — including the causes of the other person’s action, who was also moved by their own passions. Understanding weakens anger’s hold and gives you back your freedom to choose.
anger.practice: Try describing the situation that angers you as a researcher would: what causes and passions might have been driving the other person? This isn’t an excuse — just a view from the side.

quote.text: Hate is increased by reciprocal hate, and can, on the other hand, be destroyed by love.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

shame.text: “Not to laugh, not to weep, not to curse, but to understand” — this was the rule by which Spinoza studied people. Shame is agonizing, and everyone who cares about how they live feels it. Spinoza defined shame as sadness accompanied by the idea of some action of ours that we imagine others condemn. He didn’t consider shame a virtue, but he granted it something good: shame shows that the desire to live honorably is alive in a person. Yet the heart of Spinoza’s approach is his gaze without condemnation. You can turn that same gaze on yourself: your action had causes, and so do your feelings. Understanding doesn’t cancel responsibility, but it lets you look at yourself not as a defendant, but as a living being who is learning.
shame.practice: Describe what you’re ashamed of in the third person, in a calm tone, as a scientist would: “they did this because…”. What changes?

quote.text: I have taken great care not to laugh at human actions, not to mourn them, and not to curse them, but to understand them.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

guilt.text: A stone set in motion by a push, if it were conscious, would think it was flying of its own free will — that is how Spinoza explained to a friend the illusion of free decision. Your guilt tells you that acting well matters to you. Spinoza called a close affect “repentance” — sadness accompanied by the idea of some deed we believe we did from a free decision of the mind. His view here is unusual: Spinoza held that a person’s actions follow from a chain of causes, and the illusion of an “absolutely free decision” only deepens the torment. He even remarked that the one who repents is wretched twice over: first because of the deed, and then because of the sadness about it. Understanding is more useful than punishing yourself: sort out the causes, and then turn your strength toward acting differently.
guilt.practice: Imagine your action as that very stone and name to yourself the pushes that sent it on its way: circumstances, feelings, not-knowing. Then — one thing you want to do now, building on that understanding.

envy.text: Spinoza found a good which, he said, can belong to everyone at once and doesn’t shrink by being shared — understanding. Envy is a very human feeling, and he explains it without reproach. For him, envy is a kind of hatred in which another’s happiness saddens us and another’s misfortune pleases us. It is born of comparison: the imagination places us next to someone else, and their good seems like our loss. Where the good is common, there is no room for envy. This doesn’t mean outward goods don’t matter. But you can understand envy as a signal of your own desire — and remember that there are goods no one can take from you by gaining them for themselves.
envy.practice: Ask yourself: what do I actually want when I envy? Is there something in this desire that isn’t taken from anyone else if I have it too?

emptiness.text: “Each thing, as far as it can by its own power, strives to persevere in its being” — this proposition of Spinoza’s may matter most on days when you want nothing. Emptiness and apathy are a heavy state, and it isn’t your fault. He called this striving conatus. He believed this striving is the very essence of a thing. Even when you feel nothing and want nothing, the conatus in you hasn’t disappeared — it is just very quiet, like a fire under ash. The fact that you’re reading these lines, looking for understanding, is already a sign of it. Spinoza believed that the power to live grows from joy, even the smallest, and from understanding. So there’s no need to wait for a great surge of inspiration: it’s enough to notice one tiny “a little better” and let it be.
emptiness.practice: Find one very small thing that makes you even half a degree warmer: tea, light, a sound. Give it one minute.

quote.text: Each thing, as far as it can by its own power, strives to persevere in its being.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

confusion.text: Spinoza earned his living grinding lenses — work in which cloudy glass becomes clear step by step. Confusion is when your picture of the world has broken into fragments and everything looks as if through cloudy glass. Spinoza distinguished “adequate” ideas — clear ones, in which we see the causes — from “inadequate” ones, that is, muddled and fragmentary ideas we pick up through chance experience and other people’s opinions. He didn’t consider muddle a disgrace: at first, most of anyone’s ideas are exactly like that. The path to clarity, for Spinoza, is a gradual clearing-up of connections: what follows from what, what depends on what. He built the Ethics itself step by step, from the simple to the complex. Your confusion is the moment you noticed that the old fragments don’t fit together. And that is already the beginning of understanding, not its absence.
confusion.practice: Choose one part of the situation you feel at least a little sure about, and say it out loud. Then ask, as Spinoza does in the Ethics: what follows from this?

fatigue.text: In the Ethics, a book built like geometry, a list of pleasures suddenly appears: pleasant food and drink, scents, green plants, music, games, theater. Your tiredness is an honest signal from the body, and Spinoza treated the body with respect: for him, mind and body are two sides of one being. When the body is drained, the mind’s power to act weakens too. Spinoza was no stern ascetic. It befits a wise person, he wrote, to refresh and restore themselves with all of this in moderation — with everything that can be enjoyed without harm to others. He believed that only grim superstition forbids a person to rejoice. Rest and pleasure are not a weakness or a reward “for merit,” but a condition for your power to live to recover.
fatigue.practice: Pick one simple thing from Spinoza’s list — music, plants, a good cup of tea, a game — and allow it to yourself today, without feeling you have to earn it.

boredom.text: Spinoza, his biographer tells us, spent his hours of rest drawing portraits of acquaintances in ink and charcoal. Everyone knows boredom, and it doesn’t make you any worse. Spinoza has no separate teaching on boredom, but his ideas let us say something important about it. He observed that the human body is made of many parts and needs varied nourishment and experience for all its abilities to stay alive. He also saw that affects often get stuck on a single object and narrow our world. In this light, boredom can be understood as a signal: your power to act has been left idle; it lacks variety and connection with what feeds it. This isn’t a reason to reproach yourself, but an invitation to check which side of your nature hasn’t been given room for a long time.
boredom.practice: Take a pencil and spend a couple of minutes drawing something in front of you, as Spinoza did in his hours of rest. Meanwhile ask yourself: which of my abilities hasn’t been fed in a long while?

joy.text: Spinoza, often pictured as a cold geometer, wrote that laughter and jest are a pure good, as long as there is no mockery in them. Joy is what he wished for people more than anything. He defined it as a passage to greater perfection, that is, to a greater power of living and acting. Joy literally makes you more alive. Spinoza distinguished joy that takes hold of just one part of us from “cheerfulness” — joy that fills the whole being; of the latter he wrote that it cannot be excessive and is always good. So there’s no need to eye your joy with suspicion or wait for the moment you’ll “have to pay for it.” Let it be: for Spinoza, this is your nature acting freely.
joy.practice: Notice how joy changes your body: your breathing, your shoulders, your face. Stay with that sensation for a few breaths.

love.text: In a single line — “joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause” — Spinoza defined love, and there is more warmth in this formula than it seems. The tenderness you feel is a warm and very important feeling. We love what increases our power to live, and we connect that joy with a particular person or thing. That is why, he explains, the one who loves naturally strives to have the beloved near and to keep it safe. Tenderness is care for what makes the world more alive for us. Spinoza especially valued love grounded in understanding rather than imagination alone: it is steadier, because it sees the other as they really are. Your tenderness is a sign that the power of joy is at work in you.
love.practice: Tell someone you love, today, which of their traits makes you “more alive.” One sentence is enough.

gratitude.text: “Only free people are truly grateful to one another,” Spinoza writes in the Ethics, and it is one of his warmest propositions. Your gratitude is one of the brightest feelings. Spinoza defined it as a desire, born of love, to do good to the one who has done good to us. For him it is a natural continuation of joy: we love the cause of our joy and want to answer it in kind. The free are those guided by reason rather than calculation or fear. Their gratitude isn’t like an exchange of favors: it is friendship. Your gratitude isn’t a debt to be repaid, but a bond that strengthens you both. You can simply feel it and, if you like, express it.
gratitude.practice: Name one person you’re grateful to right now and one specific thing they did. Do you feel like telling them somehow?

hope.text: “All things excellent are as difficult as they are rare” — Spinoza ends the Ethics with this sentence, and what you hear in it is not hopelessness but a calm hope. Hope is a life-giving feeling that helps you keep going. Spinoza defined it as an inconstant joy arising from the image of a future thing whose outcome we doubt. He was honest: since the outcome is doubtful, hope always lives next door to fear. That’s why he wrote that hope in itself is not yet the highest good — it tells us how much we don’t know. For Spinoza, as uncertainty shrinks and we better understand what we can do, hope can grow into “confidence” — a calm joy that doesn’t depend on swings. You can cherish your hope and, little by little, turn it into understanding: what here is within my power?
hope.practice: Name what you hope for, and today do one small thing in that direction — something already within your power.

quote.text: There is neither hope without fear, nor fear without hope.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Affects, Explanation of 13

nostalgia.text: For the feeling you have now, Spinoza has a Latin word — desiderium — and a definition as precise as a technical drawing. Nostalgia is a subtle feeling in which love and sadness meet. “Longing” (desiderium), for Spinoza, is a desire to possess a thing, kept alive by the memory of it and at the same time held back by the memory of other things that exclude its existence. Put simply: memory calls us back there, and the knowledge that that time is gone holds us back. Hence both the sweetness and the bitterness. Spinoza helps us see that nostalgia is the work of memory and love. It shows that you were once happy, and that you have the capacity for that kind of joy. You don’t need to bring the past back to find in it a clue about what is dear to you.
nostalgia.practice: Remember what you miss and ask yourself: what feeling was at the heart of that time — lightness, closeness, freedom? Where could it find a place now?

craving.text: “An affect can be restrained only by an opposite and stronger affect,” Spinoza stated, and this dry proposition holds a whole strategy. A sharp “I want it right now” can be very strong. Spinoza looked at desire without condemnation: he called it the very essence of a human being, an expression of conatus — the striving to live and preserve oneself. The trouble isn’t the desire itself, but the way imagination ties it to a single object and paints that object as the only path to relief. Spinoza noted that an affect toward a thing we imagine as near and available “now” is stronger than one toward a future thing, even a far more important one. So it helps not to argue with the craving, but to look beside it for something living that gives you strength, however small.
craving.practice: Name the relief you’re expecting from this right now — calm, warmth, rest — and think about what else could give you even a little of it.

quote.text: An affect cannot be restrained or taken away except by an affect opposite to, and stronger than, the affect to be restrained.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

addiction.text: Spinoza titled the fourth part of the Ethics “Of Human Bondage” — meaning not chains but the power of the passions, which everyone knows. Addiction is not a moral failure. He would have called it one form of that bondage: a state in which we are governed by external causes and passions rather than by our own understanding. For Spinoza, bondage is the common lot of humankind, not the fault of one individual. At the opening of his unfinished Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect, he honestly admits that he himself had seen how the pursuit of wealth, honor and sensual pleasure can take over the mind so completely that it can hardly think of anything else. The path to freedom, for Spinoza, runs not through self-flagellation but through gradually understanding your affects and seeking joys that strengthen rather than empty you.
addiction.practice: Recall what the thing your addiction is organized around gave you at the very beginning — not as an excuse, but as a first step toward understanding. If you feel like it, talk about this with someone who knows this path from the inside, for example in a mutual-help group.

quote.text: Man’s lack of power to moderate and restrain the affects I call bondage.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

hangover.text: “The drunk believes he speaks from a free decision of the mind things that, once sober, he would rather have kept to himself” — an example from Spinoza’s Ethics. A hangover morning is hard on both body and soul: anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. Spinoza would say there is nothing mysterious here. For him the mind is “the idea of the body”: when the body’s power decreases, so does the mind’s, so this morning’s dark thoughts are largely dictated by an exhausted body. He gave this example not as a reproach, but to show how little free we are when external causes move us. Understanding this lifts some needless weight from the soul: yesterday’s “you” acted under a strong influence, and today’s “you” can calmly sort things out once you’ve recovered.
hangover.practice: Today, just one thing: water, food, rest. If conversations about yesterday are needed, put them off until you feel stronger.

euphoria.text: Spinoza has two words for joy: hilaritas, “cheerfulness,” which fills the whole being, and titillatio, “titillation,” which seizes just one part. A burst of euphoria is a strong joy, and for him joy is a passage to a greater power of living. Cheerfulness, for Spinoza, cannot be excessive, while titillation can flare up so strongly that it blocks out everything else. This isn’t a reason to spoil your celebration. Rather, it’s a way to live it more attentively: to notice whether the high fills you wholly — body, thoughts, relationships — or seizes just one side. That attention in itself, for Spinoza, makes joy more your own, more active — and therefore more lasting.
euphoria.practice: Look inside yourself: where is this joy felt — in your body, in your thoughts, in the wish to share it with someone? Just notice.

crash.text: “Joy is a person’s passage from a lesser perfection to a greater, sadness from a greater to a lesser,” Spinoza defines, and the key word here is “passage.” A sharp drop after a high is painful, and it isn’t your fault. He saw them not as states but as movements. The crash is a movement, not a new truth about you and your life. It feels especially sharp because imagination compares “now” with the peak you’ve just lived through. Spinoza advised looking into the causes of an affect: what exactly lifted you, and what has changed. As the causes become clearer, the crash stops feeling like the world collapsing and becomes an understandable ebb after the tide.
crash.practice: Tell yourself: “Things feel harder right now because…” — and name one specific cause, not a verdict on yourself. That is already a small passage toward clarity.

panic.text: Among the affects Spinoza also described “consternation” — fear so strong that astonishment at the danger paralyzes the very wish to escape it. Right now a wave of terror is sweeping over you, and your body seems to slip out of control. It’s an honest admission: fear can be so strong that it keeps us from even moving. But Spinoza also offers something to lean on: mind and body are two sides of one being, and everything that happens in the body is reflected in the mind. So what helps isn’t arguing with the terror, but returning to the body — to what it feels right now. A wave like this usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You don’t need to decide anything — just breathe and wait.
panic.practice: Give your body a clear, simple impression: press your feet into the floor, put a hand on your chest or belly, and take a few breaths with a long, slow exhale. Name out loud three things you can see.

dread.text: Imagine a little worm living in the blood, Spinoza suggested in a letter: it would see only separate particles and never guess they are all parts of one vast body. The question “what’s the point of it all” and the feeling of an abyss come to thoughtful people. Spinoza answered it with his whole philosophy. For him a human being is part of infinite Nature, one of its living expressions, and the essence of each of us is conatus, the striving to live. It’s an invitation to change where you’re looking from: the abyss looks like an abyss when we see ourselves as separate and alone. But when we understand ourselves as part of a large, living whole, the question “what for?” gets a simple answer: to live, to act and to rejoice — as far as it is in our power.
dread.practice: Name one thing that adds to your power to live today — a person, a sound, an activity. Stay with it in your mind for a minute.

quote.text: A free man thinks of nothing less than of death, and his wisdom is a meditation on life, not on death.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

fomo.text: Spinoza turned down a professorship at Heidelberg to keep his freedom of thought, and stayed on grinding lenses in a small Dutch town. The fear of missing out is a very human feeling: it seems that everyone else is living more vividly, and you’re not where it’s happening. He noticed that chasing honor and recognition forces us to live with an eye on people’s opinions: to seek what they seek and avoid what they avoid. Later, in the Ethics, he called the immoderate desire for glory “ambition” and showed how it feeds on the imitation of others’ affects: we want what we imagine others want. The fear of missing out isn’t your personal flaw but a mechanism of the imagination. You can notice it and ask: do I want this myself, or do I just see that others want it?
fomo.practice: Pick one “I should be there” and ask yourself, like Spinoza turning down the professorship: if no one ever found out about it, would I want it? Answer honestly, even if only to yourself.

sleepless.text: We imagine the sun as if it were about two hundred feet away, Spinoza observed — and even knowing the truth, we go on seeing it as near. Lying awake with thoughts going round is exhausting, and at night the imagination is just as stubborn as with that sun. He wrote that the mind imagines a thing as present until the body receives an impression that excludes its existence. During the day there are plenty of such “excluding” impressions: people, tasks, light. At night there are almost none, and imagined troubles freely take up all the space, as if they were happening right now. This doesn’t mean you see the truth more clearly — on the contrary, you see it less well. Understanding this mechanism can loosen the grip of night thoughts a little: they are loud, but no more reliable than they are by day.
sleepless.practice: Give your body one real, “excluding” impression: feel the fabric of the blanket, the coolness of the pillow, the weight of your hands. Stay with that sensation.

betrayal.text: Hatred of what we once loved can be greater than if we had never loved at all — this proposition of the Ethics holds a great deal of sad experience. Betrayal wounds deeply because the blow comes from someone you loved or trusted. Spinoza described exactly why it hurts so much. To such hatred, he explained, sadness over the lost love is added. So the strength of your pain is a measure of how open you were. Spinoza did not demand immediate forgiveness. He suggested gradually coming to understand — both your own feelings and the causes that moved the other person. Understanding doesn’t justify the betrayal, but it slowly gives you back the strength that powerless hatred takes away.
betrayal.practice: Name to yourself what exactly in this story was valuable to you — trust, closeness, a shared purpose. That is what you still have, even if the person is gone.

jealousy.text: What here is fact, and what is a picture the imagination paints again and again? Spinoza would begin the conversation with that question. Jealousy is agonizing, and he described it with rare precision. He defined it as a vacillation of mind in which love and hatred for the beloved live side by side, mixed with envy toward a rival. Jealousy is especially hard, he observed, because the imagination paints painful pictures of its own accord and returns to them again and again. Spinoza didn’t shame this feeling — he saw it as a natural consequence of a love that depends on what doesn’t belong to us. His path is understanding: telling apart what you actually know from what imagination fills in. This doesn’t make your love smaller, but it reduces the power of pictures that torment you more than the facts do.
jealousy.practice: When a painful picture comes, name it: “this is an image, not a fact.” Then shift your gaze to something real in front of you.

resentment.text: Spinoza advised preparing for wrongs in advance: learning a few rules of living by heart and returning to them often, so they are at hand when needed. An old grudge is a weight you carry against your will. Spinoza would take it seriously: you were hurt, and sadness accompanied by the idea of its cause is exactly what he defined as hatred. He suggested not clinging to the image of the offense, but understanding that people’s actions follow from a chain of causes — and answering wrongs not with hatred but with nobility. Spinoza noted that a mind that understands things as necessary suffers less from them. Letting go of a grudge here means not forgiving out of duty, but ceasing to hand over your power to live to it. This happens gradually, and there’s no need to hurry.
resentment.practice: Describe the grudge in one sentence the way a calm historian would: what happened and what causes might have been behind it.

heartbreak.text: Spinoza opens the Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect with an admission: people suffer most from loving what is changeable and not in their power. A broken heart hurts, and the pain shows how much this person meant to you. Spinoza defined love as joy connected with the idea of its external cause. When the cause goes away, the joy doesn’t vanish without a trace at once: memory calls us again and again to where things were good. This isn’t a reproach for having loved — that is how all people love. But it is a hint: alongside a love that wounds, you can grow joys no one can take away — understanding, friendship, your own pursuits. They won’t replace what was lost, but they will give your heart something to rest on.
heartbreak.practice: Name one joy that belongs to you alone and doesn’t depend on the relationship that ended. Give it a little time today.

impostor.text: For Spinoza, self-abasement and pride are mirror-image errors: one thinks less of oneself than is fair, the other more, and both are born of vague ideas about oneself. The fear of being found out — “I’m not who they take me for” — torments a great many people, clever and experienced ones included. — is felt by very many people, clever and experienced ones included. Spinoza has a precise word for one part of it: “self-abasement” — when, under the influence of sadness, a person thinks less of themselves than is fair. Its opposite is “self-esteem,” a joy born when a person clearly sees their real power of acting. This isn’t overconfidence but sobriety. Try looking at yourself as a researcher, not as a defendant: what can you actually do, and what do you actually do?
impostor.practice: Recall three specific things you’ve done well — not impressions of yourself, but facts. Say them out loud.

self_hatred.text: “Each thing, as far as it can by its own power, strives to persevere in its being,” Spinoza writes in the Ethics. Self-hatred is a very heavy feeling, and the inner critic can speak loudly and convincingly. But Spinoza would not agree with it. For him the essence of every person is conatus, the striving to live, and by its very nature it aims at preserving and strengthening oneself, not against oneself. If a voice inside you hates you, then for Spinoza it is the result of external causes: other people’s words, hurts you’ve lived through, images absorbed long ago. Such a voice doesn’t reveal the truth about you; it shows what has happened to you. Spinoza believed that self-esteem grounded in understanding is perhaps the highest thing we can hope for. The way to it isn’t punishment, but understanding yourself without mockery or curses.
self_hatred.practice: Ask your inner critic: “Whose voice are you speaking in?” Say out loud whose voice it reminds you of — this helps separate it from you.

helplessness.text: “Human power is very limited and is infinitely surpassed by the power of external causes” — so begins one of the most consoling passages of the Ethics. Helplessness is a heavy experience, and Spinoza knew perfectly well that human beings are not all-powerful. So, he writes at the end of the fourth part, we cannot adapt everything outside us to our use. But he adds a consolation that helps many people: if we understand that we did what was in our power, and that our power could not reach further, then the better part of us can calmly accept what happens. This isn’t passivity. It’s an honest distinction: here is where my possibilities end — and here is what, within that boundary, I still can do. Helplessness before something large doesn’t cancel your strength in something small.
helplessness.practice: Say out loud: “This is not in my power, and it is not my fault. But here is what I can do today: …” — and do that one small action.

procrastination.text: “I see the better and approve it, but I follow the worse” — Spinoza quoted this line of Ovid to explain why knowledge by itself doesn’t get us moving. When you can’t get started, it’s easy to mistake it for laziness, though laziness isn’t the problem. Spinoza described the mechanism of this state precisely. True knowledge of what is good, he wrote, cannot by itself restrain an affect — only insofar as it becomes an affect itself, that is, takes on the color of feeling. That’s why pep talks of the “I must, I must” kind usually don’t work: they remain knowledge without force. What works is something else — finding even a drop of joy, interest or relief in the task. Spinoza helps you stop shaming yourself and look not for more discipline, but for more living feeling connected with the beginning.
procrastination.practice: Find in this task one part that could be even a tiny bit interesting or pleasant for you — and start with exactly that part.

uprooted.text: At twenty-three Spinoza was expelled for ever from the Jewish community of Amsterdam in which he had grown up — with a ban on anyone even coming near him. Being cut off from home is a deep loss, and he knew it firsthand. Later he left Amsterdam and lived in small Dutch towns, earning his living by grinding lenses. He lost his former circle, but he built a new one — of friends and interlocutors with whom he corresponded and argued. In his philosophy a human being is part of one Nature, and that belonging doesn’t depend on a city or a country: wherever you are, you remain part of the whole. But Spinoza also held that nothing is more useful to a person than another person. Roots in a new place grow not through the landscape but through connections.
uprooted.practice: Name one person in your new place you’d like to talk with a little more. Think about what small step toward that is possible this week.

overload.text: When there are too many images, Spinoza wrote, they blur into a vague general “something” — and the mind stops telling one thing from another. Overload from an endless stream of information is a real burden on the mind, not your weakness. He wrote that the human body can distinctly perceive only a limited number of images at once. Any beyond that begin to blur together. For Spinoza this was a property of the body’s nature, not a flaw of character. The mind, for Spinoza, is strong not through the number of its images but through the clarity of the links between them. Hence a simple conclusion: clarity returns when there are fewer images. You don’t need to keep up with everything — you need to give your mind a chance to see one thing distinctly again.
overload.practice: Put the screen aside for five minutes and look closely at one object nearby, the way a lens grinder looks at glass: its shape, color, texture. Let your mind see one thing whole.

unreality.text: “The mind is the idea of the body” — this short formula of Spinoza’s hides an address you can use to find your way back to reality. When the world or you yourself seem not quite real, it is frightening. Here Spinoza offers something to lean on in his central idea about human beings. We know ourselves and the world first of all through how the body feels and responds. When the link with bodily sensations seems to weaken, the world can seem flat and distant, like a picture. The way back leads not through thinking about whether everything is real, but through simple sensations: warmth, weight, touch, breath. The body is your most direct connection with reality, and in it you always have a point of presence.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a distinct texture — wood, fabric, cool glass. Describe to yourself three sensations you feel.

awe.text: Deus sive Natura — “God, or Nature”: Spinoza joined these words with a single “or,” and everything that exists turned out to be part of one infinite whole. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare experience, and worth treasuring. Spinoza described “wonder” as a state in which the mind lingers on something singular, because that image resembles nothing familiar and isn’t connected with others. And love for what we wonder at he called “devotion.” But Spinoza also offers a deeper dimension of awe: what he called “the intellectual love of God” — the joy of understanding how everything in Nature is connected. For him, awe before the world doesn’t contradict reason; it can become its summit. Your awe is a moment when you felt yourself part of something immense. Let it last.
awe.practice: Try to notice what the thing that stirred your awe is connected with: where it came from, what it is a part of. Stay in that sense of connection.

relief.text: “Joy accompanied by the idea of a past thing that turned out better than we had hoped” — this is how Spinoza defined gladness, gaudium. Right now you seem to be feeling exactly that — a bright relief. There is an important detail in this definition: relief always carries the memory of fear. That’s exactly why it is felt so strongly — the joy here is measured by how tense the waiting was. For Spinoza every joy is a passage to a greater power of living, so relief literally gives you back your strength. There’s no need to rush on or to devalue it with “it could have been worse.” Allow yourself this passage — body and mind recover precisely in moments like these.
relief.practice: Notice what strength has come back to you along with the relief: what do you feel like doing now, what do you have more energy for?

calm.text: Spinoza devoted the last pages of the Ethics to what he called “true peace of mind” — the whole book had been leading there. The calm you feel is a precious state. The wise person, who understands themselves and the world as part of the necessary order of Nature, he wrote, is rarely troubled in spirit. An important thought of Spinoza’s: this calm is not a reward to be earned, nor a lull before the storm. It is itself the good — what he called blessedness. Calm here isn’t emptiness or indifference: it is a clarity in which joy becomes quiet and steady. If you feel it now, there’s no need to ask “how long will it last.” You can simply be in it and notice how it is made.
calm.practice: Sit in silence for a minute, doing nothing. Notice what thoughts, sensations or circumstances accompany your calm, and remember at least one of them.

quote.text: Blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

inspiration.text: “No one has yet determined what the body can do,” Spinoza wrote, and there is more hope in that sentence than in many hymns. Inspiration is one of the most joyful states, and he would explain why it feels the way it does. He distinguished affects that we “undergo” from external causes from joy that arises out of our own activity — when we ourselves are the cause of what happens. Inspiration is a moment when your conatus acts freely and at full strength: you aren’t being pushed; you are creating. Spinoza believed that human abilities are wider than we usually think. Allow yourself this lift. It shows you what strength is in you — and that it can appear again.
inspiration.practice: Write down what exactly inspires you now, and where you feel yourself to be the cause rather than a spectator. Mark the first small step.

quote.text: No one has yet determined what the body can do.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part III, Scholium to Proposition 2

schadenfreude.text: Spinoza took this feeling apart without a shadow of reproach: if we hate or envy someone, their imagined misfortune brings us joy. Almost no one admits to schadenfreude, though almost everyone knows it. That is exactly how he defined envy — as sadness at another’s happiness and joy at another’s misfortune. So schadenfreude isn’t a sign that you’re rotten, but the trace of another, earlier affect: a hurt, envy, a sense of injustice. Spinoza would add: such joy is fragile, because it depends on other people’s falls rather than on your own strength. It helps neither to chase it away nor to be ashamed of it, but to ask: what pain in me has just found relief?
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself who this person is to you and what happened between you before. What old feeling — a hurt, envy, weariness from comparison — stands behind today’s joy?

contempt.text: “Less than is fair” — these three words in Spinoza’s definition turn contempt from a verdict on another into an error of vision. It can be cold and even pleasant: it seems to set us above the other. Spinoza distinguished two affects here. “Disregard” — when a thing touches the mind so little that we notice in it what isn’t there rather than what is. And “scorn” (despectus) he defined as thinking less of someone than is fair, out of hatred. It usually grows out of being hurt: the person caused us sadness, and the imagination shrinks them. This isn’t a reason to reproach yourself. But you can check: what do I know about the causes that made this person the way they are? Understanding causes, Spinoza said, gradually frees us from the need to look down on others — and from the weariness that comes with it.
contempt.practice: Name to yourself three facts about the person you feel contempt for, without judgment — just what they do and in what circumstances. Notice whether anything in the feeling shifts.

disgust.text: Anything, Spinoza wrote, can “by accident” become a cause of sadness for us — simply because it once happened to be near something that affected us. Disgust is an ancient, bodily feeling: you want to pull away, shut yourself off, not see. Spinoza explained it very soberly. Hence his definition: “aversion” (aversio) is sadness accompanied by the idea of a thing that has accidentally become its cause. In other words, disgust often says more about our history than about the object itself. This applies to disgust with yourself too: it may also be a trace of old associations and other people’s words, not the truth about you. Spinoza didn’t demand that we force ourselves to love what repels us. He suggested understanding which associations the feeling is made of — and then it stops being a verdict.
disgust.practice: Let one question sit with you: what else in my life is this image or person connected with? Let the first association simply come, without judging it.

revenge.text: “Hatred is increased by reciprocal hatred and, on the contrary, can be destroyed by love” — this proposition of Spinoza’s sounds almost like a sermon, though it was derived geometrically. The wish for revenge is a natural response to pain inflicted on you, and Spinoza didn’t pretend it doesn’t exist. He defined “vengeance” as the desire by which, from reciprocal hatred, we are moved to do harm to someone who has harmed us. Spinoza proposed another path — not as a moral demand, but as a path to your own strength: to answer hostility with “nobility,” that is, with an action of reason that strengthens us ourselves. This doesn’t mean the hurt doesn’t matter. It means you can hear out the wish for revenge as a cry for justice — and look for a form for it that won’t take away your freedom.
revenge.practice: Ask yourself: what does my wish for revenge really want — acknowledgment, justice, safety? What small step toward that is possible without harming anyone?

quote.text: He who lives according to the guidance of reason strives, as far as he can, to repay the other’s hate, anger, and disdain, etc., toward him, with love, or nobility.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

anger_at_loved.text: The more closely a person is woven into our life, the more strongly they can affect us — with joy and with sadness alike: that is how Spinoza would explain why those closest to us anger us most. Being angry at the people you love is one of the most ordinary experiences — and one of the most shameful-feeling. Spinoza noticed something else: we get angrier when we believe the other “freely” chose to hurt us, and softer when we see the necessary causes of their actions. Your partner, parent or child is also moved by their nature, their tiredness, their fears — just as you are. Understanding this doesn’t make your anger “wrong.” It helps you not turn it into words and actions you’ll regret later, and to see it as a signal: something here matters to me.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger at someone close rises again, say to yourself: “there are causes for this — theirs and mine.” Take three slow breaths out before you respond.

ambivalence.text: Fluctuatio animi, “vacillation of mind” — this is what Spinoza called the state in which one and the same thing is connected for us with both joy and sadness. Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them is neither strange nor hypocritical. In that state we love and hate at once, and, as in doubt, the mind is pulled in two directions. Most often this happens precisely with those close to us: we share too many joys and too many wounds with them. Spinoza didn’t demand that we choose one feeling and renounce the other. He suggested distinguishing: which particular traits, actions and memories bring joy, and which bring sadness. When the mixture comes apart into understandable pieces, it stops being an agonizing riddle and becomes a map of your relationship.
ambivalence.practice: Hold out your hands palms up: in your mind, place on one what gladdens you in this person, and on the other what wounds you. Don’t look for a total — just hold both.

guilty_relief.text: Joy, for Spinoza, is a passage to a greater power of living, and it doesn’t ask permission when it comes after a long strain. Relief after a breakup, after someone leaves, or after a loved one’s long illness often comes together with shame: “how can I feel this?” When a long stretch of strain, fear or powerlessness ends, the returning strength is inevitably felt as relief. This doesn’t mean you didn’t love: the sadness of loss and the joy of release from a burden can live in you at the same time, because they are tied to different sides of one story. Spinoza tried not to mock or curse human affects, but to understand them. Your relief is a signal of how much strength what you went through was taking, not a verdict on your love.
guilty_relief.practice: Say two sentences out loud: “It’s easier for me because … has ended” and “It hurts because I loved…”. Let both be true.

indifference.text: One and the same object, Spinoza wrote, affects different people differently — and even one person differently at different times. If an event “ought” to move you, yet inside there is silence, it’s frightening: have you gone cold? Spinoza looked at this more calmly. An affect isn’t an obligation or a test of your humanity, but an event that arises from the meeting of your body and mind with the world in a particular state. Tiredness, overload, old pain can muffle the response. Indifference, too, is a state with its own causes, not an empty space. Asking about its causes is more honest than acting out a feeling that isn’t there. Often the response comes later, once the soul has the strength.
indifference.practice: Notice to yourself what state you’re in: how much you’ve slept, how much has piled up on you lately. Name it without reproach — like the weather in which the event happened.

escape.text: “The virtue of a free person is seen as much in avoiding dangers as in overcoming them,” Spinoza wrote, and he did not consider leaving cowardly. The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your familiar role — tells you that somewhere your power to live is being squeezed. Spinoza would call this the work of conatus, the striving to preserve and strengthen one’s being: the mind, he wrote, strives to imagine what increases its power and to push away what diminishes it. So the dream of escape isn’t weakness but an understandable signal. Spinoza did, however, distinguish fleeing from sadness from moving toward joy. The first is governed by an external cause, which can follow us anywhere; the second rests on understanding what actually nourishes us. What matters is understanding what you’re moving away from and what you’re moving toward.
escape.practice: Picture, in two or three details, the place or life you want to escape to. What exactly is there — quiet, freedom, respect? Where could even a drop of it be possible this very week?

forbidden_attraction.text: “We do not desire something because we judge it good; on the contrary, we judge it good because we desire it” — one of Spinoza’s boldest observations. Attraction to someone who is unavailable or “the wrong person” often brings confusion and guilt. Spinoza suggested looking at desire without the usual moral court. Desire, he wrote, is the very essence of a human being: it is our striving to exist, conscious of itself. So the attraction itself says nothing yet about what is “right”; it says something about you — about what in you is looking for life. Spinoza would give no order here, either to act or to forbid yourself to feel. He would suggest understanding: what image, what promise of joy does this person hold for you? A desire that is understood stops steering us blindly.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Without naming the person, ask yourself: what quality or feeling in them draws me? Where else in my life could it find a place?

quote.text: We neither strive for, nor will, neither want, nor desire anything because we judge it to be good; on the contrary, we judge something to be good because we strive for it, will it, want it, and desire it.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part III, Scholium to Proposition 9

social_anxiety.text: “Nothing is more useful to a human being than another human being,” Spinoza wrote — but he also saw how easily that usefulness turns into dependence on other people’s eyes. Fear of people and their judgment can grip you so tightly that it’s hard to say a word. Spinoza explained it through a mechanism he called “the imitation of the affects”: we involuntarily take on the feelings of those who are like us, and that’s why we pick up their joy or displeasure so keenly. From this comes the striving to do what we imagine will please people. The word “imagine” matters: we react not to what others think, but to what our imagination paints. He suggested shifting your footing: from imagined judgments to clear knowledge of your own actions and of what is dear to you.
social_anxiety.practice: After spending time with people, name to yourself one thing you actually saw or heard, and one thing you only imagined about what others were thinking. Compare them.

uncertainty.text: Sub specie aeternitatis — “under the aspect of eternity”: this is how Spinoza suggested looking at things when they seem like chaos. When it’s unclear what will happen, the mind rushes between options, and that is exhausting. Feelings about a future we are unsure of swing between hope and fear. But Spinoza also offered an unexpected support. The more we understand things as necessary — as the results of chains of causes rather than whims of chance — the less we suffer from the affects. This isn’t fatalism or “nothing can be done.” It’s a view in which you see that whatever happens will have causes, many of which are already at work, and some of which are you yourself, your actions. This is the highest form of such a view — calm and wide. Uncertainty doesn’t disappear, but it stops looking like chaos.
uncertainty.practice: Draw three columns: what is already known, what depends on me, what doesn’t depend on me right now. Choose one action from the middle column.

quote.text: Insofar as the mind understands all things as necessary, it has a greater power over the affects, or is less acted on by them.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

waiting.text: Spinoza put off publishing the Ethics, and the book appeared only after his death — and while it lay in his desk, he went on grinding lenses, writing to friends and thinking. Waiting is a strange state: life seems to be on pause, while your thoughts keep running ahead. Spinoza noticed that images of the future act on us through the imagination: it either inflates them or tosses us between “it’ll work out” and “it won’t.” He believed that reason can relate to the future and the present more evenly, not letting an event that hasn’t yet happened take over your whole life. You go on living and acting now, and the joy of a small action in which you yourself are the cause is real today. There’s no need to hurry the waiting; you can simply give it back its proper place among other things.
waiting.practice: Choose one small task that depends only on you and can be finished today. Do it, and notice how your own action feels against the background of waiting.

regret.text: “Repentance is not a virtue,” Spinoza wrote, and explained: the one who repents suffers twice. Regret over what you did or didn’t do can come back again and again. Spinoza looked at it strictly, but — strange as it may seem — in a freeing way. First from the deed, then from the sadness about it. This isn’t a call to indifference. Spinoza valued understanding highly: seeing what causes — not knowing, fear, tiredness, circumstances — led to that choice. Given the causes at work back then, the past could not have been otherwise; but your understanding has changed now, and it is already changing the future. Regret is useful exactly to the extent that it turns into knowledge rather than endless self-punishment.
regret.practice: Write down: what did I know and feel back then, when I made that decision? And what do I know now that I didn’t know then?

quote.text: Repentance is not a virtue, or does not arise from reason; instead, he who repents what he did is twice miserable, or lacks power.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza

longing.text: When we remember someone, Spinoza wrote, we involuntarily want to bring back the whole picture — that place, that light, the circumstances in which we were happy with them. Missing a particular person hurts, and it is one of the few feelings Spinoza defined directly. He called it desiderium: a desire to possess a thing, kept alive by the memory of it and at the same time held back by the memory of what excludes its presence. The whole mechanics of longing is in this definition: memory brings the person back to you again — their voice, their habits — and immediately runs into the fact that they aren’t here. Longing, then, is the other side of love, of a joy that is still in you. There’s no need to chase it away; it tells you that this bond is still alive.
longing.practice: Remember one specific moment with this person — the place, the light, the words. Stay with it for a minute, then notice which quality of that moment is especially dear to you.

world_pain.text: Someone moved to help others neither by reason nor by pity, Spinoza wrote, is rightly called inhuman. Heavy news, war, injustice wound anyone who can feel, and your pain for the world is natural. Spinoza explained it through “the imitation of the affects”: when we imagine the suffering of a being like us, we feel sadness ourselves. He called this feeling “pity,” and his assessment of it was honest to the point of discomfort: sadness in itself, for Spinoza, diminishes our power, and the one who lives by reason strives not so much to suffer along as to actively help. Your pain is a sign of your humanity. Spinoza would help you take the next step: to turn it from powerless sadness into action, however small — and to protect your strength, because only someone who has strength can carry something to others.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small, real action for others — to help, support, share — and do it. Then limit your news time for today.

quote.text: He who is moved to aid others neither by reason nor by pity is rightly called inhuman.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.source: Ethics, Part IV, Scholium to Proposition 50

rejection.text: Abjectio, “self-abasement,” Spinoza defined as an opinion of oneself, born of sadness, that is lower than is fair. When you are rejected, it seems that it wasn’t an offer, a friendship or a job that was turned down, but you as a whole. Spinoza would help separate these things. After a refusal, sadness easily turns into exactly this. The words “lower than is fair” matter: this is a distortion, not the truth about you. The other person’s decision flows from their nature, history, circumstances and desires — a long chain of causes in which you are only one link. According to Spinoza, we suffer less from what we understand as the result of necessary causes rather than as a verdict. A refusal tells you how two different natures met at a particular moment — but it doesn’t measure your worth.
rejection.practice: Name out loud three things you can do or have done well, regardless of this person.

abandonment.text: An affect connected with many different causes is less burdensome than one chained to a single cause — this observation of Spinoza’s sounds like a builder’s advice: more supports. The fear of being abandoned keeps you on edge: every silence seems like a sign, every delay like a threat. Spinoza saw fear as a sadness that grows from doubt: the future is unclear, and imagination paints the worst outcome. He also noticed that we worry most about what we love when it is changeable and not fully in our power. And people are never fully in our power. When all your joy rests on one person, any step they take aside feels like a cliff edge. When it has many supports — friendship, work, the body, understanding — your love for this person remains, but fear loses its absolute power.
abandonment.practice: Draw yourself in the center of a page and connect yourself with lines to everything that gives you joy and support: people, activities, places. Look at how many connections there are.

unrequited.text: There is not a word about reciprocity in how Spinoza defined love: it is joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause. Unrequited love hurts in a special way: the feeling is alive, but there is no answer. Love is your joy, and it is real even if the other person doesn’t share it. The pain comes from the fact that, when we love, we naturally strive to be loved in return, and when that striving meets refusal, sadness arises. Spinoza would remind you: the other person follows their own nature, and another’s love can’t be summoned by effort or by merit. That is bitter, but also freeing — you haven’t failed an exam. Your capacity to love like this is a strength that belongs to you, and it doesn’t vanish because it found no answer here.
unrequited.practice: Put into a few words what exactly this love awakened in you — which qualities, desires, strengths. That is yours, and it will stay with you.

humiliation.text: Self-respect that rests only on the opinion of the crowd, for Spinoza, has to be anxiously defended every day — that is how fragile it is. Humiliation burns: it seems you’ve been made smaller — in front of others or in your own eyes. Spinoza would help you see what it is made of. We involuntarily take on other people’s feelings, he wrote. So when we are treated with disdain, we begin to look at ourselves through their eyes and feel toward ourselves what we imagine they feel. A steadier support is one grounded in understanding your own actions. It’s important to separate the event from the conclusion: you were treated in a humiliating way — that is a fact about the other person’s action. “I am worthless” is someone else’s affect that for a moment you took for your own.
humiliation.practice: Say two sentences to yourself: what exactly happened — and what conclusion about yourself this event is pressing on you. Note that the second is not a fact, but someone else’s view.

body_shame.text: Beauty and ugliness, Spinoza wrote in the appendix to the first part of the Ethics, are ways of imagining, not properties of the things themselves. Dissatisfaction with your body can be painful and exhausting. Spinoza offered a view that changes the very framing of the question. For him mind and body are not a master and a faulty tool, but one and the same being seen from two sides: the mind is the idea of the body. Waging war on your body means partly waging war on yourself. People call things beautiful or ugly depending on how they affect their imagination. The yardsticks used to judge bodies change from era to era. A more reliable question, following Spinoza: what can this body do? What does it let you feel and do?
body_shame.practice: Name three things your body has let you do or feel over the past week — without any judgments about appearance.

illness.text: Spinoza ground lenses for years and, many believe, breathed in glass dust; he suffered from a lung illness for a long time, yet worked as far as his strength allowed. When the body lets you down, it isn’t only the body that suffers: your mood, your thoughts, your sense of yourself change too. Spinoza explained this by the unity of mind and body: whatever diminishes the body’s power to act diminishes the mind’s power to think as well. So tiredness, irritability and sadness during illness aren’t a weakness of character but a natural consequence. He didn’t promise that understanding would heal the body. But he showed that even within limits there remains room for activity: understanding what is happening, noticing the small joys that are still within reach, being the cause of at least a few small events in your day.
illness.practice: Today, notice one small action in which you yourself are the cause: you chose what to read, whom to write to, how to sit more comfortably. That, too, is your strength.

pride.text: Acquiescentia in se ipso, “self-esteem,” was for Spinoza perhaps the highest thing we can hope for. Pride in something you’ve done is a good feeling, and he would be glad for you. He distinguished two very different affects. “Pride” in the sense of arrogance — thinking more highly of yourself than is fair, born of self-love and fed by comparison with others. And “self-esteem” (acquiescentia in se ipso) — a joy that arises when a person contemplates themselves and their power of acting. Spinoza valued the second very highly. The difference is simple: arrogance needs someone below, while self-esteem needs only a clear view of your own action. You did something, and you are its cause. Let yourself see that and be glad: such joy, for Spinoza, doesn’t puff a person up — it makes them stronger and more generous.
pride.practice: Jot down which of your qualities it took to do what you did. Read it through and give yourself a minute simply to be glad.

melancholy.text: Spinoza reserved the word “melancholy” for a heavy sadness that takes hold of the whole person, and he considered it always harmful. Bright sadness, in which sorrow mingles with tenderness and memory, works differently. In Spinoza’s terms, the affects in it are mixed: sadness over what has passed or is out of reach, and joy in the memory itself, in beauty, in love for what was lost. It is precisely this joy that makes the sadness “bright.” Spinoza advised understanding your affects, and understanding, in his view, brings joy of its own. So there’s no need to fear this state: stay in it for a while, make out the love in it — and notice that it doesn’t take from you, but in its own way nourishes you.
melancholy.practice: What is this sadness about, and what in it is dear to you? Write down one word for the sorrow and one for the tenderness.
